sermon.title: God’s Word to Rebellious People
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer teaches from Isaiah 29 and 30 about God punishing His people and their opponents, and says believers must confront opposition to the Bible, drawing examples from Moses, Joshua, Daniel, Jesus and Paul and from church history and the Humanist Manifesto. He closes with God’s promise “in that day” to rebels who repent: He opens ears and eyes, answers their cry, and says “weep no more.”

Editor note: he says “Chapter 30:2” where the quoted words (“Because you have rejected this message”) are Isaiah 30:12; the caption words are kept as spoken. The statements about the Catholic Church, the Humanist Manifesto, politics, homosexuality and church history are his own and are not verified here; the Humanist Manifesto and magazine quotations are as he read them. chunks.section_question: What does Isaiah 29 say about God punishing His people and their opponents, and honoring Him with lips only? (Isaiah 29:1-13)
chunks.short_answer: He says Isaiah 29 gives “a word about God punishing the city of God, the people of God, Jerusalem, and her opponents,” both those God used to correct His people and those who just oppose God and His people. He says those who fight God and His church are like a man who dreams he eats but wakes up still hungry, and that we can say we are believers while “the heart, the mind, the will, our actions, our attitude is removed far from God.”
chunks.text:
Okay, in Isaiah 29:1-17 we find God, through Isaiah, giving a word about God punishing the city of God, the people of God, Jerusalem, and her opponents: those that God used to correct his people, and those that just oppose God and his people. It says in verse one, “Woe to Ariel, the city where David dwelt.” That’s Jerusalem. Woe to Jerusalem, you will be brought down.

He said in verse 7, “The multitude of the nations that fight against Jerusalem, Ariel, shall be as a dream of a night.” When a man dreams and he’s hungry and he eats, he’s thirsty and he drinks, but he wakes up, he’s still hungry and he’s still thirsty. It’s just a dream. So people that think they can fight against God and his church, they’re just it’s just a dream. It says you will be punished by the Lord who fight against Mount Zion, the church. Isaiah 29:10, “The Lord has closed your eyes, and the eyes of the prophets, and the eyes of your rulers and the seers has he covered. The vision is like words of a sealed book delivered to one who’s learned, saying, ‘Read this,’ and he says, ‘I can’t read it because it’s sealed.’ Delivered to another that’s not learned, and he says, ‘I can’t read it because I’m not learned.’”

For this reason the Lord says, “As the people draw nigh to me with their mouth and their lips do honor me, but they have removed their heart far from me.” You see, yeah, we say we’re believers, yeah, we say we’re Christians, but the heart, the mind, the will, our actions, our attitude is removed far from God. “Their fear toward me is taught by the precept of men.” You see, and do we have that today, where we just teach our own doctrines, man-made doctrines, much like the Constitution of America’s interpreted for their own personal gain, so is the Bible in a generation we live in. it’s just And when people use the word “interpret,” watch out, because the Bible doesn’t need to be interpreted. The Bible interprets itself. It explains itself. You don’t have to psychoanalyze it.

chunks.section_question: How do the fruits of righteousness make us a light to the world? (Philippians 1:10-11, Matthew 5:16)
